```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
# Bash chunks are a record of commands you ran in the Terminal. Knitting shows
# them but doesn't run them again.
knitr::opts_hooks$set(engine = function(options) {
  if (options$engine == "bash") options$eval <- FALSE
  options
})
```

Notes for [Workshop 1](https://mb5370.bioinformatics.guide/workshop1.html). Run the commands for this workshop in the Terminal, from inside the `command_line` folder:

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/command_line
pwd
```

Replace the text below each heading with your own notes. Copy each command you run into a bash chunk like the one above.

## Basic unix commands

Notes on `pwd`, `ls`, `cd` and how unix commands are put together.

**ls**

```{r}
ls # shows files
ls -l # lists files in long format
ls -lr # lists files as in long format -r revers sorts the files
ls -lrh #
```

```{r}
ls -l/usr #/usr tells the terminal what directionary to pull from
```

```{r}
ls /home/ #shows all the users in the rstudio = our class
```

**cd**

```{r}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/command_line # cd tells the terminal where to go /where we want to be, sort of gives us the opertunity to place ouself in the righ location in the files and folders. 
```

```{r}
cd .. # moves up in the directry
```

**pwd**

```{r}
pwd # Showes us where in the folders and files we are lockated 
```

## Viewing and searching files

Notes on `cat`, `head`, `grep` and `man`.

**cat**

```{r}
cat test.fasta # Showes the content of the file
```

**head**

```{r}
head -2 test.fasta # head displayes the first 10 lines of the file, but the -2 only displays the first 2 lines
```

**grep**

```{r}
grep '^>' test.fasta # the grep comand finds specific lines in files.
```

```{r}
grep KDRNKKNSAK test.fasta # for example here we ask to find a specific amino acid sequence (KDRNKKNSAK) in the test.fasta file
```

```{r}
grep -n KDRNKKNSAK test.fasta # this one searches the file and shows the line number the sequence is on
```

**man**

```{r}
man grep # to se usefull flags we use the man command to veiw them. 
```

some useful flags include:

-i -\> case insensitive match

-n -\> report line number of matches

-c -\> count all files that contain the pattern

-w -\> match whole words only

## Sequence file formats

Notes on the fasta and fastq formats.

**fasta** - often used for "refrence data

**fastaq** - most commonly used for "raw" reads from next generation sequencing experiments.

## Redbean Assembly

```{r}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/redbean # navigate to the redbean folder
```

```{r}
cat /pvol/data/amtp4/*_[012].fastq > amtp4.fastq # 
```

Run the asembly

```{r}
wtdbg2 -x ont -g 5m -t 4 -i amtp4.fastq -fo amtp4
wtpoa-cns -t 4 -i amtp4.ctg.lay.gz -fo amtp4.ctg.fa # takes a few minutes to run this assembly
#does 6 coverage of the target genome
```

**Activity:** Inspect assembly statistics

```{r}
assembly-stats amtp4.ctg.fa 
```

shows: stats for amtp4.ctg.fa

sum = 4031799, n = 133, ave = 30314.28, largest = 143785 N50 = 51901, n = 23 N60 = 41852, n = 31 N70 = 28222, n = 44 N80 = 21358, n = 59 N90 = 13591, n = 83 N100 = 2697, n = 133 N_count = 0 Gaps = 0

**How good does the assembly look in terms of contiguity and completeness?**

n=133 means it is fairly fragmented, a finished bacterial genome would be one or a few pieces.

**Run redbean with higher coverage**

```{r}
cat /pvol/data/amtp4/*.fastq > amtp4_20x.fastq
wtdbg2 -x ont -g 5m -t 4 -i amtp4_20x.fastq -fo amtp4_20x
wtpoa-cns -t 4 -i amtp4_20x.ctg.lay.gz -fo amtp4_20x.ctg.fa # data equivalent ot aroud 20x coverage
#takes a bit (a lot) longer 
```

**Activity:** Inspect assembly stats for higher coverage

```{r}
assembly-stats amtp4_20x.fastq
```

result: sum = 159325343, n = 40000, ave = 3983.13, largest = 42815 N50 = 7147, n = 6711 N60 = 5719, n = 9200 N70 = 4455, n = 12358 N80 = 3248, n = 16524 N90 = 2008, n = 22665 N100 = 109, n = 40000 N_count = 0 Gaps = 0

**Activity:** Inspect low coverage flye assembly with Bandage

In this visualisation contiguous segments are shown as solid coloured lines. Some of these are separated into independent graphs whereas others (eg the mess in the top left) are connected to each other via black lines. There are few things to keep in mind here;

1.  Biologically distinct entities such as chromosomes or plasmids will form separate graphs

2.  Separated graphs can also occur if coverage is very low and no reads exist to join parts of the assembly together

3.  Highly joined regions (eg top left) tend to occur because repeats create ambiguities. There are too many connections and the assembler has trouble choosing the correct path between them.

## **Check Assembly Quality with QUAST**

Use this command to look at the contig sizes in the flye assembly

```{r}
cat ../flye_genome/amtp4_20x/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx '{print $name, length($seq)}' | sort -n -k2
```

for me the longest were cotig_59 and contig_10

Note that you will need to modify this command by replacing `XX` and `YY` with the contig numbers of the two longest contigs in your assembly.

```{r}
samtools faidx ../flye_genome/amtp4_20x/assembly.fasta contig_59 contig_10 > flye_asm/vibrio.fasta
```

Now do the same for redbean

```{r}
cat ../redbean/amtp4_20x.ctg.fa | bioawk -c fastx '{print $name, length($seq)}' | sort -n -k2
samtools faidx ../redbean/amtp4_20x.ctg.fa ctg1 ctg2 > redbean_asm/vibrio.fasta
```

ctg2 1764939

ctg1 3343994

my two longest
